en.heading: Overview
en.body: Shakespeare’s tragedy of a Scottish general who murders his way to the crown. Macbeth by William Shakespeare opens its world slowly, letting you settle into its place and people before it puts the central question in front of you.

en.heading: How the story begins
en.body: The opening scene looks ordinary, yet it carries the seed of everything that follows. You meet the first relationships and places, and notice small details that later turn out to be keys to the whole story. With each chapter the pace tightens and the characters’ choices narrow.

en.heading: Key figures
en.body:
• Macbeth — Thane of Glamis. A brave Scottish general whose ambition is stirred by a prophecy.
• Lady Macbeth — His wife. His wife and fiercest partner, sharp-minded and unafraid of what ambition demands.
• Banquo — General and friend. Macbeth’s friend and fellow general: honest, steady and watchful.
• Duncan — King of Scotland. The gracious king, who trusts those closest to him.
• The Witches — The weird sisters. Three strange sisters who meet Macbeth on the heath with a prophecy.
• Macduff — Thane of Fife. A Scottish nobleman, loyal to his country and its rightful order.

en.heading: Rising action
en.body: By the middle of the book the threads are tangled: decisions that seemed small open doors that cannot be shut, and relationships shift from closeness to rivalry or from doubt to certainty. The narration moves between what characters think and what they actually do, and the gap between the two is where much of the book’s power lives.

en.heading: Big themes
en.body: The reading circles around classic, tragedy, ambition, power. The book asks about power, justice, belonging and memory without handing you ready answers; it leaves you with its contradictions and trusts you to weigh them.

en.heading: Climax and ending
en.body: The action peaks when each character has to face the consequences of what they chose. I will not give away the details here, but the ending reorders everything you read before it and gives it deeper meaning.

en.heading: Why it is worth reading
en.body: It pairs a plot that holds you with language that stays with you, and its questions still feel close today. If it grabs you, start with the characters, then return to the scenes that stopped you.

en.heading: Questions to carry while you read
en.body:
• Who really holds the power in the story?
• What do the characters lose when they win?
• Which scene changed meaning on a second read?

en.heading: Overview
en.body: Dickens’s novel of London and Paris in the years of the French Revolution. A Tale of Two Cities by Charles Dickens opens its world slowly, letting you settle into its place and people before it puts the central question in front of you.

en.heading: How the story begins
en.body: The opening scene looks ordinary, yet it carries the seed of everything that follows. You meet the first relationships and places, and notice small details that later turn out to be keys to the whole story. With each chapter the pace tightens and the characters’ choices narrow.

en.heading: Key figures
en.body:
• Sydney Carton — A London barrister. Brilliant, careless and unhappy, until love gives his life a purpose.
• Charles Darnay — A French émigré. A nobleman who renounces his family’s cruelty and makes a new life in England.
• Lucie Manette — The golden thread. Doctor Manette’s daughter, whose tenderness holds the story together.
• Madame Defarge — Revolutionary of Saint Antoine. She knits the names of the condemned into her register and never forgets.

en.heading: Rising action
en.body: By the middle of the book the threads are tangled: decisions that seemed small open doors that cannot be shut, and relationships shift from closeness to rivalry or from doubt to certainty. The narration moves between what characters think and what they actually do, and the gap between the two is where much of the book’s power lives.

en.heading: Big themes
en.body: The reading circles around classic, revolution, french, london. The book asks about power, justice, belonging and memory without handing you ready answers; it leaves you with its contradictions and trusts you to weigh them.

en.heading: Climax and ending
en.body: The action peaks when each character has to face the consequences of what they chose. I will not give away the details here, but the ending reorders everything you read before it and gives it deeper meaning.

en.heading: Why it is worth reading
en.body: It pairs a plot that holds you with language that stays with you, and its questions still feel close today. If it grabs you, start with the characters, then return to the scenes that stopped you.

en.heading: Questions to carry while you read
en.body:
• Who really holds the power in the story?
• What do the characters lose when they win?
• Which scene changed meaning on a second read?
Ask Bayan any time to go deeper into a chapter or a character.

en.heading: Overview
en.body: A detective story in the Macmillan Readers series for learners of English. The Woman Who Disappeared by Philip Prowse opens its world slowly, letting you settle into its place and people before it puts the central question in front of you.

en.heading: How the story begins
en.body: The opening scene looks ordinary, yet it carries the seed of everything that follows. You meet the first relationships and places, and notice small details that later turn out to be keys to the whole story. With each chapter the pace tightens and the characters’ choices narrow.

en.heading: Key figures
en.body:
• The Detective — Private investigator. Patient, observant and hard to fool, the narrator of the case.
• The Client — The one who asks for help. The person who brings the case, and may know more than they say.
• The Missing Woman — At the centre of the mystery. Everyone describes her differently; finding her means understanding her.

en.heading: Rising action
en.body: By the middle of the book the threads are tangled: decisions that seemed small open doors that cannot be shut, and relationships shift from closeness to rivalry or from doubt to certainty. The narration moves between what characters think and what they actually do, and the gap between the two is where much of the book’s power lives.

en.heading: Big themes
en.body: The reading circles around mystery, crime, detective, easy. The book asks about power, justice, belonging and memory without handing you ready answers; it leaves you with its contradictions and trusts you to weigh them.

en.heading: Climax and ending
en.body: The action peaks when each character has to face the consequences of what they chose. I will not give away the details here, but the ending reorders everything you read before it and gives it deeper meaning.

en.heading: Why it is worth reading
en.body: It pairs a plot that holds you with language that stays with you, and its questions still feel close today. If it grabs you, start with the characters, then return to the scenes that stopped you.

en.heading: Questions to carry while you read
en.body:
• Who really holds the power in the story?
• What do the characters lose when they win?

en.heading: Overview
en.body: A portrait of Riyadh, from its palm-filled valleys to the capital it became. Riyadh: Heart of Arabia by King Fahd National Library collection opens its world slowly, letting you settle into its place and people before it puts the central question in front of you.

en.heading: How the story begins
en.body: The opening scene looks ordinary, yet it carries the seed of everything that follows. You meet the first relationships and places, and notice small details that later turn out to be keys to the whole story. With each chapter the pace tightens and the characters’ choices narrow.

en.heading: Key figures
en.body:
• The Historian — Keeper of the city’s story. Knows how Riyadh grew, from oasis to capital.
• The Traveller — A visitor from the past. Describes old Riyadh as early travellers saw it.

en.heading: Rising action
en.body: By the middle of the book the threads are tangled: decisions that seemed small open doors that cannot be shut, and relationships shift from closeness to rivalry or from doubt to certainty. The narration moves between what characters think and what they actually do, and the gap between the two is where much of the book’s power lives.

en.heading: Big themes
en.body: The reading circles around riyadh, city, history, heritage. The book asks about power, justice, belonging and memory without handing you ready answers; it leaves you with its contradictions and trusts you to weigh them.

en.heading: Climax and ending
en.body: The action peaks when each character has to face the consequences of what they chose. I will not give away the details here, but the ending reorders everything you read before it and gives it deeper meaning.

en.heading: Why it is worth reading
en.body: It pairs a plot that holds you with language that stays with you, and its questions still feel close today. If it grabs you, start with the characters, then return to the scenes that stopped you.

en.heading: Questions to carry while you read
en.body:
• Who really holds the power in the story?
• What do the characters lose when they win?
• Which scene changed meaning on a second read?
Ask Bayan any time to go deeper into a chapter or a character.

en.body: The opening scene looks ordinary, yet it carries the seed of everything that follows. You meet the first relationships and places, and notice small details that later turn out to be keys to the whole story. With each chapter the pace tightens and the characters’ choices narrow.

en.heading: Key figures
en.body:
• The City Planner — Drawing tomorrow’s Riyadh. Explains the plans that shaped the modern city.
• The Resident — Grew up with the city. Remembers the neighbourhoods before and after.

en.heading: Rising action
en.body: By the middle of the book the threads are tangled: decisions that seemed small open doors that cannot be shut, and relationships shift from closeness to rivalry or from doubt to certainty. The narration moves between what characters think and what they actually do, and the gap between the two is where much of the book’s power lives.

en.heading: Big themes
en.body: The reading circles around riyadh, city, urbanism, planning. The book asks about power, justice, belonging and memory without handing you ready answers; it leaves you with its contradictions and trusts you to weigh them.

en.heading: Climax and ending
en.body: The action peaks when each character has to face the consequences of what they chose. I will not give away the details here, but the ending reorders everything you read before it and gives it deeper meaning.

en.heading: Why it is worth reading
en.body: It pairs a plot that holds you with language that stays with you, and its questions still feel close today. If it grabs you, start with the characters, then return to the scenes that stopped you.

en.heading: Questions to carry while you read
en.body:
• Who really holds the power in the story?
• What do the characters lose when they win?
• Which scene changed meaning on a second read?
Ask Bayan any time to go deeper into a chapter or a character.
